claims.evidence: This is supported by crystal structure data (Figure 7) and ITC binding data showing KD of ~5 µM.

claims.claim: The first crystal structures of Salmonella Typhimurium Tsr in complex with L-serine have been reported.
claims.source: We report the first crystal structures of Salmonella Typhimurium Tsr in complex with L-serine and identify a conserved amino acid recognition motif for L-serine shared among Tsr orthologues.
claims.evidence: Crystal structures were solved at 2.2 Å resolution (PDB: 8FYV) and 2.5 Å resolution (PDB: 8VL8).

claims.claim: A conserved amino acid recognition motif for L-serine is shared among Tsr orthologues.
claims.source: We report the first crystal structures of Salmonella Typhimurium Tsr in complex with L-serine and identify a conserved amino acid recognition motif for L-serine shared among Tsr orthologues.
claims.evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data in Figure 8A showing conservation of ligand-binding pocket residues.

claims.claim: Tsr is widely conserved among Enterobacteriaceae.
claims.source: We find Tsr to be widely conserved among Enterobacteriaceae and numerous World Health Organization priority pathogens associated with bloodstream infections.
claims.evidence: This is supported by genomic database analysis shown in Figure 8B and Supplementary file 2.

claims.claim: Tsr is conserved among numerous World Health Organization priority pathogens associated with bloodstream infections.
claims.source: We find Tsr to be widely conserved among Enterobacteriaceae and numerous World Health Organization priority pathogens associated with bloodstream infections.
claims.evidence: This is supported by genomic database analysis identifying Tsr in WHO priority pathogen genera (Figure 8B).

claims.claim: Enterobacteriaceae use human serum as a source of nutrients for growth.
claims.source: Lastly, we find that Enterobacteriaceae use human serum as a source of nutrients for growth and that chemotaxis and the chemoreceptor Tsr provide a competitive advantage for migration into enterohemorrhagic lesions.
claims.evidence: This is supported by growth curve data in Figure 6 showing 1.5-2.5-fold growth increase with serum addition.

claims.claim: Chemotaxis and the chemoreceptor Tsr provide a competitive advantage for migration into enterohemorrhagic lesions.
claims.source: Lastly, we find that Enterobacteriaceae use human serum as a source of nutrients for growth and that chemotaxis and the chemoreceptor Tsr provide a competitive advantage for migration into enterohemorrhagic lesions.
claims.evidence: This is supported by ex vivo swine colonic lesion experiments showing WT outcompetes cheY and tsr mutants (Figure 8J-M).

claims.claim: Bacterial vampirism is defined as bacterial behavior of taxis toward serum, colonization of hemorrhagic lesions, and consumption of serum nutrients.
claims.source: We define this bacterial behavior of taxis toward serum, colonization of hemorrhagic lesions, and the consumption of serum nutrients as 'bacterial vampirism', which may relate to the proclivity of Enterobacteriaceae for bloodstream infections.
claims.evidence: This is a conceptual definition proposed by the authors based on their experimental observations.

claims.claim: Bacterial vampirism may relate to the proclivity of Enterobacteriaceae for bloodstream infections.
claims.source: We define this bacterial behavior of taxis toward serum, colonization of hemorrhagic lesions, and the consumption of serum nutrients as 'bacterial vampirism', which may relate to the proclivity of Enterobacteriaceae for bloodstream infections.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative connection proposed by the authors based on their findings.

claims.claim: Most bacterial genera classified by WHO as 'priority pathogens' employ chemotaxis systems for efficient infection.
claims.source: Previously, we determined that most bacterial genera classified by the World Health Organization (WHO) as 'priority pathogens' employ chemotaxis systems for efficient infection and exert precise control over their colonization topography (Zhou et al., 2023; Murray et al., 2022; Tacconelli et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Severe GI bleeding affects around 40-150 out of every 100,000 individuals annually.
claims.source: Although severe GI bleeding is not a typical outcome of enteric infection, it is a substantial burden on human health, affecting around 40–150 out of every 100,000 individuals annually, with a fatality rate ranging from 6% to 30% (Figure 1; Zhou et al., 2023; Tacconelli et al., 2018; Aljarad and Mobayed, 2021; Huang et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2014; Moledina and Komba, 2017; Saltzman, 2022; Scales and Huffnagle, 2013).
claims.evidence: This epidemiological data is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: GI bleeding has a fatality rate ranging from 6% to 30%.
claims.source: Although severe GI bleeding is not a typical outcome of enteric infection, it is a substantial burden on human health, affecting around 40–150 out of every 100,000 individuals annually, with a fatality rate ranging from 6% to 30% (Figure 1; Zhou et al., 2023; Tacconelli et al., 2018; Aljarad and Mobayed, 2021; Huang et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2014; Moledina and Komba, 2017; Saltzman, 2022; Scales and Huffnagle, 2013).
claims.evidence: This mortality data is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Enterobacteriaceae are prone to bloodstream entry.
claims.source: Enterobacteriaceae are prone to bloodstream entry and are a leading cause of sepsis-related deaths in individuals with inflammatory bowel diseases (IBDs) that have recurrent enterohemorrhagic lesions (Weber et al., 2020; Goren et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical literature.

claims.claim: The CIRA microgradient is established through injection at a constant rate of ~300 fl/min through a 0.5 µm glass microcapillary.
claims.source: The CIRA microgradient is established through injection at a constant rate of ~300 fl/min, through a 0.5 µm glass microcapillary, and expands over time through diffusion (Figure 2A and B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a methodological description supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: A millimolar source recedes to nanomolar concentrations after diffusion across only a few hundred microns in the CIRA system.
claims.source: We calculate that the introduction of a minute volume of novel effector produces a steep microgradient, in which a millimolar source recedes to nanomolar concentrations after diffusion across only a few hundred microns (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by mathematical modeling and experimental validation with A488 dye (Figure 2B-D).

claims.claim: A bacterium 100 µm from a 1 mM infinite-volume source experiences a local concentration of approximately 10 nM after 300 s of injection.
claims.source: For instance, in our assay we expect a bacterium 100 µm from a 1 mM infinite-volume source to experience a local concentration of a small molecule effector (diffusion coefficient approximately 4 × 10−6 cm2 s–1) of 10 nM after 300 s of injection (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is calculated from the diffusion model presented in the methods.

claims.claim: The bacterial population in proximity to the serum source doubles by 40 s post-treatment.
claims.source: By these metrics, we determined S. Typhimurium IR715 is attracted to human serum. The bacterial population in proximity to the serum source doubles by 40 s, reaches a maximal attraction rate by 90 s, and approaches equilibrium by 300 s post-treatment (Figure 2G).
claims.evidence: This is quantified from CIRA experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claims.claim: The bacterial population reaches a maximal attraction rate by 90 s post-treatment with serum.
claims.source: By these metrics, we determined S. Typhimurium IR715 is attracted to human serum. The bacterial population in proximity to the serum source doubles by 40 s, reaches a maximal attraction rate by 90 s, and approaches equilibrium by 300 s post-treatment (Figure 2G).
claims.evidence: This is quantified from CIRA experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claims.claim: The bacterial population approaches equilibrium by 300 s post-treatment with serum.
claims.source: By these metrics, we determined S. Typhimurium IR715 is attracted to human serum. The bacterial population in proximity to the serum source doubles by 40 s, reaches a maximal attraction rate by 90 s, and approaches equilibrium by 300 s post-treatment (Figure 2G).
claims.evidence: This is quantified from CIRA experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claims.claim: All tested Salmonella serovars showed attraction responses to human serum.
claims.source: In varying magnitude, all strains showed attraction responses to human serum, seen as a significant distribution bias toward the serum source relative to the experiment periphery (Figure 3, Video 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by CIRA competition experiments shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Chemotaxis is responsible for the rapid localization of S. enterica to human serum.
claims.source: Thus, we determined that chemotaxis is responsible for the rapid localization of S. enterica to human serum.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experiments showing cheY mutants do not exhibit attraction (Figure 4G).

claims.claim: The tsr mutant has deficiencies in serum attraction but does not eliminate it completely.
claims.source: Since tsr mutation diminishes serum attraction but does not eliminate it, we conclude that multiple chemoattractant signals and chemoreceptors mediate taxis to serum.
claims.evidence: This is supported by CIRA competition experiments showing tsr mutants have reduced but not absent attraction (Figure 4H-I).

claims.claim: Multiple chemoattractant signals and chemoreceptors mediate taxis to serum.
claims.source: Since tsr mutation diminishes serum attraction but does not eliminate it, we conclude that multiple chemoattractant signals and chemoreceptors mediate taxis to serum.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that tsr mutants retain some attraction to serum.

claims.claim: Treatment of serum with serine racemase diminishes attraction of S. Typhimurium IR715.
claims.source: The attraction of S. Typhimurium IR715 to serum treated with serine racemase is diminished and the population is more diffuse (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by CIRA experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: S. Typhimurium shows no chemoattraction response to norepinephrine (NE).
claims.source: We observed robust chemoattraction responses to L-serine, evident by the accumulation of cells toward the treatment source (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E, Video 4), but no response to NE or DHMA, with the cells remaining randomly distributed even after 5 min of exposure (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–I, Videos 5 and 6).
claims.evidence: This is supported by CIRA experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F-I and Videos 5 and 6.

claims.claim: S. Typhimurium shows no chemoattraction response to DHMA.
claims.source: We observed robust chemoattraction responses to L-serine, evident by the accumulation of cells toward the treatment source (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E, Video 4), but no response to NE or DHMA, with the cells remaining randomly distributed even after 5 min of exposure (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–I, Videos 5 and 6).
claims.evidence: This is supported by CIRA experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F-I and Videos 5 and 6.

claims.claim: The minimal source concentration of L-serine needed to induce chemoattraction is 0.5-5 µM.
claims.source: Within the 5 min timeframe of our experiments, the minimal source concentration of L-serine needed to induce chemoattraction is 0.5–5 µM.
claims.evidence: This is determined from dose-response CIRA experiments shown in Figure 5D-E.

claims.claim: The K1/2 for L-serine chemoattraction is approximately 105 µM.
claims.source: The [L-serine] source required for half-maximal chemoattraction (i.e., K1/2) is approximately 105 µM (Figure 5D and E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is calculated from dose-response data shown in Figure 5D-E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The typical concentration of L-serine in human serum is >200-fold greater than the minimum required to elicit chemoattraction.
claims.source: Therefore, we determined that the typical concentration of L-serine in human serum is >200-fold greater than the minimum required to elicit chemoattraction.
claims.evidence: This is calculated from the measured serum L-serine concentration (~241 µM) and the minimal effective concentration (0.5-5 µM).

claims.claim: The tsr mutant shows no chemoattraction to L-serine.
claims.source: However, we found when treated with L-serine, the tsr mutant showed no chemoattraction and behaved similarly to the chemotaxis-null cheY mutant (Figure 5G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by CIRA experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claims.claim: The tsr mutant mounts a robust chemoattraction response to L-aspartate similar to wildtype.
claims.source: We found that the tsr mutant mounted a robust chemoattraction response to 500 µM L-aspartate, similar in magnitude and rate to WT (Figure 5G), supporting that chemotaxis to non-serine stimuli remains functional in the tsr strain.
claims.evidence: This is supported by CIRA experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claims.claim: Serum addition enhances growth of all Salmonella strains surveyed.
claims.source: In all strains surveyed, we found that serum addition enhances growth, and we saw no evidence of killing even for the highest serum concentrations tested (Figure 6).
claims.evidence: This is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: 2.5% v/v serum is sufficient to provide a 1.5-2.5-fold growth increase.
claims.source: The growth enhancement requires relatively little serum, as 2.5% v/v is sufficient to provide a 1.5–2.5-fold growth increase (Figure 6, https://public.vetmed.wsu.edu/Baylink).
claims.evidence: This is quantified from growth curve data shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Human serum samples contain 241 µM ± 48 total serine.
claims.source: We determined by mass spectrometry that our human serum samples contain 241 µM ± 48 total serine (L- and D-enantiomers), of which approximately 99% is expected to be L-serine (Hashimoto et al., 2003; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is measured by mass spectrometry as described in the methods.

claims.claim: Approximately 99% of total serine in human serum is L-serine.
claims.source: We determined by mass spectrometry that our human serum samples contain 241 µM ± 48 total serine (L- and D-enantiomers), of which approximately 99% is expected to be L-serine (Hashimoto et al., 2003; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: L-serine functions as a molecular cue that directs Salmonella toward serum.
claims.source: This leads us to believe that L-serine functions as a molecular cue that directs Salmonella toward serum, but nutrients present in serum other than L-serine provide the major growth advantages.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that L-serine alone does not recapitulate the growth benefit of serum.

claims.claim: Nutrients present in serum other than L-serine provide the major growth advantages.
claims.source: This leads us to believe that L-serine functions as a molecular cue that directs Salmonella toward serum, but nutrients present in serum other than L-serine provide the major growth advantages.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from growth experiments showing serum provides greater benefit than L-serine alone.

claims.claim: No experimentally determined structure had been published for S. enterica Tsr prior to this work.
claims.source: No experimentally determined structure had been published for S. enterica Tsr (SeTsr) and the single experimentally determined Tsr structure to have captured the L-serine-binding interactions is a crystal structure of EcTsr LBD of moderate resolution (2.5 Å, PDB: 3ATP), in which the electron density for the ligand is weak and the orientation of the L-serine ligand is ambiguous (Tajima et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature prior to this work.

claims.claim: The crystal structure of SeTsr LBD was solved at 2.2 Å resolution.
claims.source: The crystal that provided the highest quality data (2.2 Å resolution, PDB: 8FYV) was grown in a mixture of buffers of pH 7.5–9.7 (refer to 'Methods', Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is reported as a result of the crystallography experiments.

claims.claim: SeTsr and EcTsr possess 100% identity of the ligand-binding residues.
claims.source: SeTsr and EcTsr possess high-sequence similarity in the LBD region—100% identity of the ligand-binding residues and 82.1% identity over the entire periplasmic domain—and as expected, retain a similar global structure with all chains of serine-bound SeTsr (5), serine-bound EcTsr (2), and apo EcTsr (2) overlaying within 0.24 Ǻ rmsd over 139 Cα (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: This is determined from sequence alignment and structural comparison.

claims.claim: SeTsr and EcTsr possess 82.1% identity over the entire periplasmic domain.
claims.source: SeTsr and EcTsr possess high-sequence similarity in the LBD region—100% identity of the ligand-binding residues and 82.1% identity over the entire periplasmic domain—and as expected, retain a similar global structure with all chains of serine-bound SeTsr (5), serine-bound EcTsr (2), and apo EcTsr (2) overlaying within 0.24 Ǻ rmsd over 139 Cα (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: This is determined from sequence alignment.

claims.claim: L-serine binds to SeTsr LBD with a KD of approximately 5 µM.
claims.source: As expected, L-serine produces a robust exothermic binding curve, exhibiting a KD of approximately 5 µM (Figure 7K).
claims.evidence: This is measured by isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) shown in Figure 7K.

claims.claim: Norepinephrine (NE) shows no evidence of binding to SeTsr LBD.
claims.source: Conversely, neither NE nor DHMA showed any evidence of binding to SeTsr LBD (Figure 7L and M).
claims.evidence: This is measured by ITC experiments shown in Figure 7L.

claims.claim: DHMA shows no evidence of binding to SeTsr LBD.
claims.source: Conversely, neither NE nor DHMA showed any evidence of binding to SeTsr LBD (Figure 7L and M).
claims.evidence: This is measured by ITC experiments shown in Figure 7M.

claims.claim: Tsr is widely conserved among Gammaproteobacteria, particularly within the families Enterobacteriaceae, Morganelliaceae, and Yersiniaceae.
claims.source: The biological distribution of Tsr reveals the chemoreceptor to be widely conserved among Gammaproteobacteria, particularly within the families Enterobacteriaceae, Morganelliaceae, and Yersiniaceae (Figure 8B).
claims.evidence: This is determined from genomic database analysis shown in Figure 8B.

claims.claim: Many WHO priority pathogens possess Tsr.
claims.source: We discovered that many WHO priority pathogens are among the species that have Tsr, leading us to suspect these pathogens and pathobionts also perform serum taxis.
claims.evidence: This is determined from genomic database analysis shown in Figure 8B.

claims.claim: E. coli MG1655 exhibits attraction to human serum.
claims.source: We find that both these strains exhibit attraction to human serum on time scales and magnitudes similar to experiments with Salmonella (Figure 8C–E, Videos 8 and 9).
claims.evidence: This is supported by CIRA experimental data shown in Figure 8C-E.

claims.claim: C. koseri BAA-895 exhibits attraction to human serum.
claims.source: We find that both these strains exhibit attraction to human serum on time scales and magnitudes similar to experiments with Salmonella (Figure 8C–E, Videos 8 and 9).
claims.evidence: This is supported by CIRA experimental data shown in Figure 8C-E.

claims.claim: Horse serum induces rapid attraction of S. Typhimurium IR715.
claims.source: Similar to human serum, the bacterial population rapidly swam toward the horse serum source, with the relative number of cells in close proximity to the source nearly doubling within 120 s of exposure (Figure 8F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by CIRA experimental data shown in Figure 8F.

claims.claim: Pig serum induces rapid attraction of S. Typhimurium.
claims.source: The data revealed that pig serum similarly induces a rapid attraction of S. Typhimurium (Figure 8G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by CIRA experimental data shown in Figure 8G.

claims.claim: Wildtype S. Typhimurium IR715 outcompetes cheY mutant by approximately 10:1 in colonization of hemorrhagic lesions.
claims.source: Strikingly, the WT efficiently localizes toward, and migrates into, the hemorrhagic lesion, outcompeting the cheY and tsr mutants by approximately 10:1 and 2:1 (Figure 8J–M).
claims.evidence: This is quantified from ex vivo swine colonic lesion experiments shown in Figure 8J-M.

claims.claim: Wildtype S. Typhimurium IR715 outcompetes tsr mutant by approximately 2:1 in colonization of hemorrhagic lesions.
claims.source: Strikingly, the WT efficiently localizes toward, and migrates into, the hemorrhagic lesion, outcompeting the cheY and tsr mutants by approximately 10:1 and 2:1 (Figure 8J–M).
claims.evidence: This is quantified from ex vivo swine colonic lesion experiments shown in Figure 8J-M.

claims.claim: Bacteria were able to penetrate >200 µm into wounded vasculature in the ex vivo model.
claims.source: In the context of this ex vivo model, we observed that the bacteria were readily able to penetrate >200 µm into the wounded vasculature (Figure 8J–M).
claims.evidence: This is measured from z-stack imaging of ex vivo lesions shown in Figure 8J-M.

claims.claim: The attraction of Enterobacteriaceae to serum aligns with an emerging understanding of how bacterial chemotaxis can drive tropism for sites of damaged tissue, injury, and inflammation.
claims.source: In a broader context, the attraction of Enterobacteriaceae to serum aligns with an emerging understanding of how bacterial chemotaxis can drive tropism for sites of damaged tissue, injury, and inflammation (Figure 1; Zhou et al., 2023; Scales and Huffnagle, 2013; Aihara et al., 2014; Callahan et al., 2021; Croxen and Finlay, 2010; Hanyu et al., 2019; Rivera-Chávez et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is a conceptual connection supported by citations to related literature.

claims.claim: Colitis stimulates substantial increases in the luminal availability of most amino acids, with average serine content nearly doubling.
claims.source: Moreover, colitis was found to stimulate substantial increases in the luminal availability of most amino acids, with the average serine content nearly doubling (Kitamoto et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The EcTsr LBD structure (PDB: 3ATP) has the L-serine positioned incorrectly.
claims.source: With the aid of the improved view provided by our SeTsr structure, we noticed the L-serine is positioned differently than what was modeled into the weak density of the EcTsr structure (Figure 7G–I, Video 7).
claims.evidence: This is determined by comparing the SeTsr structure with the EcTsr structure and performing paired refinements (Figure 7J).

claims.claim: Substituting the serine pose from SeTsr into the EcTsr model reduces Rwork/Rfree values by -0.2%/-0.2%.
claims.source: Substituting the serine with the pose observed in the SeTsr structure led to an improved model, reducing the Rwork/Rfree values by –0.2%/–0.2%.
claims.evidence: This is determined from paired refinement analysis shown in Figure 7J.

claims.claim: Replacing both the serine ligand and ligand-binding residues of the EcTsr model with those from SeTsr reduces Rwork/Rfree values by -1.0%/-0.9%.
claims.source: Lastly, we replaced both the serine ligand and the ligand-binding residues of the EcTsr model with those from our SeTsr structure, which resulted in the highest quality model with meaningfully lower Rwork/Rfree values of –1.0%/–0.9% (Figure 7J).
claims.evidence: This is determined from paired refinement analysis shown in Figure 7J.

claims.claim: The L-serine hydroxyl sidechain donates a hydrogen bond to the Asn68 sidechain oxygen in the SeTsr structure.
claims.source: In this orientation, the ligand is in an optimal energetic conformation that satisfies all possible hydrogen bonding interactions: the positively charged peptide amine donates hydrogen bonds to the backbone carbonyl oxygens of Phe151, Phe152, and Gln154, the negatively charged ligand carboxyl group donates hydrogen bonds to the Arg64 guanidinium group, the Asn68 side change amine, and a water (W2), and the ligand hydroxyl sidechain donates a hydrogen bond to the Asn68 sidechain oxygen, and accepts a hydrogen bond from a water (W1) (Figure 7F, Video 7).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 7F.

claims.claim: The positively charged peptide amine of L-serine donates hydrogen bonds to the backbone carbonyl oxygens of Phe151, Phe152, and Gln154.
claims.source: In this orientation, the ligand is in an optimal energetic conformation that satisfies all possible hydrogen bonding interactions: the positively charged peptide amine donates hydrogen bonds to the backbone carbonyl oxygens of Phe151, Phe152, and Gln154, the negatively charged ligand carboxyl group donates hydrogen bonds to the Arg64 guanidinium group, the Asn68 side change amine, and a water (W2), and the ligand hydroxyl sidechain donates a hydrogen bond to the Asn68 sidechain oxygen, and accepts a hydrogen bond from a water (W1) (Figure 7F, Video 7).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 7F.

claims.claim: The negatively charged carboxyl group of L-serine donates hydrogen bonds to the Arg64 guanidinium group, the Asn68 side chain amine, and a water molecule.
claims.source: In this orientation, the ligand is in an optimal energetic conformation that satisfies all possible hydrogen bonding interactions: the positively charged peptide amine donates hydrogen bonds to the backbone carbonyl oxygens of Phe151, Phe152, and Gln154, the negatively charged ligand carboxyl group donates hydrogen bonds to the Arg64 guanidinium group, the Asn68 side change amine, and a water (W2), and the ligand hydroxyl sidechain donates a hydrogen bond to the Asn68 sidechain oxygen, and accepts a hydrogen bond from a water (W1) (Figure 7F, Video 7).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 7F.

claims.claim: S. Typhimurium uses the chemoreceptor Tsr to locate and invade Peyer's patches.
claims.source: S. enterica Typhimurium uses the chemoreceptor Tsr to locate and invade Peyer's patches (Rivera-Chávez et al., 2016), which could involve L-serine chemoattraction originating from serum or necrotic cells.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: GI bleeding afflicts 60% of infected children under the age of five with Salmonella infections.
claims.source: Although GI bleeding is relatively uncommon in Salmonella infections overall, it afflicts 60% of infected children under the age of five (White et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This epidemiological data is supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Neurotransmitter NE and its metabolized form DHMA are thought to circulate at approximately 10 nM.
claims.source: The concentration of L-serine in human serum ranges from approximately 100–400 µm, depending on diet and health factors (He et al., 2022; Miller et al., 2020; Pitkänen et al., 2003), whereas the neurotransmitter NE, and its metabolized form, DHMA, are thought to circulate at approximately 10 nM (Kopin et al., 1978; Steuer et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Serum contains high concentrations of glucose (5 mM) and L-serine (100-300 µM).
claims.source: Of these, by far the two most prevalent chemoattractants in serum are glucose (5 mM) and L-serine (100–300 µM) (Figure 4B–F).
claims.evidence: This is based on known serum composition and shown in microgradient modeling (Figure 4B-F).

claims.claim: The fraction of WT cells within 100 µm of the serum source increases by 70-fold in competition with cheY mutant.
claims.source: In this background, the fraction of WT cells within 100 µm of the serum source increases by 70-fold, with the maximal rate of attraction achieved by 120 s post-treatment.
claims.evidence: This is quantified from CIRA competition experiments shown in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: The maximal rate of attraction to serum is achieved by 120 s post-treatment in WT vs cheY competition.
claims.source: In this background, the fraction of WT cells within 100 µm of the serum source increases by 70-fold, with the maximal rate of attraction achieved by 120 s post-treatment.
claims.evidence: This is quantified from CIRA competition experiments shown in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: The ratio of WT to tsr cells proximal to the serum source is 3:1 by 5 min post-treatment.
claims.source: The WT efficiently outcompetes the tsr mutant such that by 5 min post-treatment the ratio of WT to tsr cells proximal to the serum source is 3:1 (Figure 4H, Video 3).
claims.evidence: This is quantified from CIRA competition experiments shown in Figure 4H.

claims.claim: Maximal attraction and dispersal rates for L-serine chemoattraction are similar, changing by approximately 4% per second.
claims.source: These experiments showed maximal attraction and dispersal rates to be similar, changing by approximately 4% per second (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: This is quantified from CIRA experiments with L-serine addition and removal shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: The CIRA microgradient concentration is accurate within 5% over the distance range 70-270 µm.
claims.source: We determined the concentration to be accurate within 5% over the distance range 70–270 µm (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is determined by comparing calculated and measured A488 concentrations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: At distances less than 70 µm from the injection site, the measured concentration is approximately 10% lower than predicted by computation.
claims.source: At smaller distances (<70 µm), the measured concentration is approximately 10% lower than that predicted by the computation. This could be due to advection effects near the injection site that would tend to enhance the effective local diffusion rate.
claims.evidence: This is observed from comparison of calculated and measured concentrations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Artifactual forces such as flow account for only minor changes to bacterial distribution at the population level, in the range of ±10%.
claims.source: Additionally, we found no behavioral differences in treatments with buffer in the range of pH 4–9, indicating small, localized pH changes are inconsequential for taxis in our system, and that any artifactual forces, such as flow, account for only minor changes to bacterial distribution at the population level, in the range of ±10% (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is determined from control experiments with different pH buffers shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Small, localized pH changes are inconsequential for taxis in the CIRA system.
claims.source: Additionally, we found no behavioral differences in treatments with buffer in the range of pH 4–9, indicating small, localized pH changes are inconsequential for taxis in our system, and that any artifactual forces, such as flow, account for only minor changes to bacterial distribution at the population level, in the range of ±10% (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is determined from control experiments with different pH buffers shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The SeTsr crystal structure has a 99th percentile all-atom MolProbity clashscore.
claims.source: The final model R/Rfree values were 24.1/25.8%, with a 99th percentile all-atom MolProbity clashscore, and a 100th percentile overall MolProbity score (Davis et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is a quality metric for the crystal structure.

claims.claim: The SeTsr crystal structure has a 100th percentile overall MolProbity score.
claims.source: The final model R/Rfree values were 24.1/25.8%, with a 99th percentile all-atom MolProbity clashscore, and a 100th percentile overall MolProbity score (Davis et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is a quality metric for the crystal structure.

claims.claim: The SeTsr structure at pH 7.5-9.7 and pH 7-7.5 are nearly identical with no observable changes at the ligand-binding site.
claims.source: By overlaying the two structures, it is apparent they are nearly identical, with no observable changes at the ligand-binding site (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).

results.result: Enterobacteriaceae species (Salmonella, E. coli, C. koseri) exhibit rapid chemotactic attraction to femtoliter volumes of human and animal serum within minutes, as demonstrated using the CIRA microfluidics assay. The bacterial population reorganizes within 40-120 seconds, with the CIRA microgradient validated to be accurate within 5-10% across relevant distances.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C4, C20-C26, C54-C57, and C78-C81 collectively demonstrate robust attraction of multiple Enterobacteriaceae species to serum from multiple mammalian sources using a validated microfluidics system. The CIRA methodology is well-characterized with appropriate controls (pH, flow artifacts), mathematical modeling, and experimental validation with fluorescent dye. Multiple independent experiments across different bacterial strains and serum sources provide converging evidence.

results.result: Chemotaxis is the primary mechanism mediating bacterial attraction to serum, with the chemoreceptor Tsr playing a significant but not exclusive role. The cheY mutant shows no attraction (70-fold difference from WT), while the tsr mutant shows reduced but not eliminated attraction (3:1 WT:tsr ratio), indicating multiple chemoreceptors contribute to serum taxis.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C27-C29, C74-C76, and C92 are supported by well-controlled competition experiments comparing WT, cheY, and tsr mutants. The cheY mutant (chemotaxis-null) shows complete loss of attraction, definitively establishing chemotaxis as the mechanism. The tsr mutant phenotype (partial defect) logically supports involvement of multiple chemoreceptors. The quantitative competitive indices provide strong effect sizes.

results.result: L-serine is the primary chemoattractant in serum sensed by Tsr, present at ~241 µM in human serum (>200-fold above the minimal effective concentration of 0.5-5 µM). Serine racemase treatment diminishes serum attraction, while NE and DHMA show no chemoattractant activity. The tsr mutant shows no attraction to L-serine but retains normal chemotaxis to L-aspartate.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C7, C30, C32-C38, C43, and C73 provide multiple lines of converging evidence: (1) mass spectrometry quantification of serum L-serine, (2) dose-response experiments establishing sensitivity thresholds, (3) serine racemase experiments showing L-enantiomer specificity, (4) negative results with NE/DHMA despite extensive testing, and (5) genetic specificity (tsr mutant phenotype specific to L-serine, not L-aspartate). The evidence is internally consistent and mechanistically coherent.

results.result: The first crystal structures of S. Typhimurium Tsr LBD in complex with L-serine were solved at 2.2 Å and 2.5 Å resolution, revealing high structural similarity to E. coli Tsr (100% identity in ligand-binding residues, 82.1% overall periplasmic domain identity, 0.24 Å rmsd). The structures show high quality metrics (99th percentile clashscore, 100th percentile MolProbity score) and full ligand occupancy.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C46-C49, C82-C87, and C89 are supported by standard crystallographic data including resolution, R-factors, validation metrics, and structural comparisons. The structures are deposited in the PDB (8FYV, 8VL8) and show appropriate quality for the stated resolution. Multiple independent views (5 monomers in asymmetric unit) and pH-independent validation strengthen confidence. The ITC binding data (KD ~5 µM) is consistent with functional assays.

results.result: The SeTsr structure reveals the correct orientation of L-serine in the binding pocket, correcting the previous EcTsr structure (PDB: 3ATP). The ligand forms optimal hydrogen bonding interactions with all binding site residues (Arg64, Asn68, Phe151, Phe152, Gln154), with the hydroxyl sidechain facing outward toward solvent. Paired refinement analysis shows that substituting the SeTsr ligand pose and binding residues into the EcTsr model improves Rwork/Rfree by -1.0%/-0.9%.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C68 are supported by rigorous crystallographic analysis including electron density maps (2fo-fc and fo-fc omit maps), paired refinement comparisons, and detailed structural characterization. The improvement in R-factors from paired refinement provides quantitative validation. The hydrogen bonding network is fully characterized and energetically favorable. This represents a significant correction to prior structural work.

results.result: Tsr is widely conserved among Gammaproteobacteria, particularly Enterobacteriaceae, Morganelliaceae, and Yersiniaceae families, including numerous WHO priority pathogens. A conserved L-serine recognition motif was identified across Tsr orthologues through sequence alignment and structural analysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C11, C52-C53 are supported by genomic database analysis (Figure 8B, Supplementary file 2) and sequence alignment showing conservation of ligand-binding residues (Figure 8A). The structural basis for defining the recognition motif is established by the crystal structure. The biological distribution analysis appears comprehensive, though the methods for database searching could be more explicitly described.

results.result: Human serum provides a growth advantage for Salmonella strains, with 2.5% v/v serum sufficient for 1.5-2.5-fold growth increase. However, L-serine alone (present at 241 µM ± 48 in serum) does not recapitulate the full growth benefit, indicating other serum nutrients are primarily responsible for growth enhancement.
results.evaluation: Claims C12, C39-C41, and C44 are supported by growth curve experiments (Figure 6) and mass spectrometry quantification of serum L-serine. The inference that L-serine functions primarily as a chemotactic cue rather than growth substrate is logical given the growth data. However, the failed serine dehydrogenase experiment limits direct testing of L-serine's nutritional contribution.

results.result: In an ex vivo swine colonic hemorrhagic lesion model, wildtype S. Typhimurium outcompetes cheY mutants by ~10:1 and tsr mutants by ~2:1 in colonization of lesions, with bacteria penetrating >200 µm into wounded vasculature. This demonstrates that chemotaxis and Tsr provide competitive advantages for migration into hemorrhagic lesions.
results.evaluation: Claims C13, C58-C60 are supported by ex vivo experiments with appropriate controls (WT vs. cheY and WT vs. tsr competitions). The competitive indices show clear and quantifiable advantages for chemotaxis-competent bacteria. However, this is a single ex vivo model with limited replicates (n=3-4), and extrapolation to in vivo infection requires caution. The model is physiologically relevant but simplified compared to actual infection.

results.result: The authors propose 'bacterial vampirism' as a conceptual framework describing bacterial taxis toward serum, colonization of hemorrhagic lesions, and consumption of serum nutrients, which may relate to the proclivity of Enterobacteriaceae for bloodstream infections. This phenomenon is suggested to be relevant across diverse host-microbe systems and may link to pathogenesis in inflammatory conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C15, C61, C90, C95-C96, C99-C100 represent conceptual synthesis and speculation based on the experimental findings. While the individual experimental observations are well-supported, the connection to actual bloodstream infections and clinical pathogenesis remains speculative. The ex vivo model provides preliminary evidence but is insufficient to establish causality in disease. The authors appropriately use cautious language ('may relate,' 'could involve,' 'seems plausible'), acknowledging the speculative nature.

results.result: Norepinephrine (NE) and DHMA show no evidence of binding to SeTsr LBD by isothermal titration calorimetry, contradicting previous reports that these neurotransmitters are Tsr ligands.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C51 are supported by ITC experiments (Figure 7L-M) showing no binding. This is further corroborated by extensive CIRA experiments (17 videos provided) showing no chemotactic response to NE or DHMA under various conditions. The negative results are convincing given the thoroughness of testing and the positive controls with L-serine. This represents an important correction to the literature.

results.result: Enterobacteriaceae are associated with GI bleeding, bacteremia, and sepsis-related deaths in individuals with inflammatory bowel diseases. GI bleeding affects 40-150 per 100,000 individuals annually with 6-30% fatality rate, and afflicts 60% of infected children under five with Salmonella infections.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C17-C19, and C70 are supported by citations to clinical and epidemiological literature. These represent established medical knowledge providing context for the study rather than novel findings. The citations appear appropriate for the claims made.

results.result: Background information from prior literature establishes that: WHO priority pathogens employ chemotaxis for infection; ~99% of serum serine is L-serine; colitis increases luminal amino acids; S. Typhimurium uses Tsr to invade Peyer's patches; NE/DHMA circulate at ~10 nM; swine share human GI physiology; and Peyer's patches are near vasculature that can be damaged.
results.evaluation: Claims C16, C42, C62, C69, C72, C91, C93-C94, C97-C98 are supported by appropriate citations to prior literature. These provide important context and rationale for the current study but are not novel findings. The citations appear accurate based on the claims made.

results.result: Maximal attraction and dispersal rates for L-serine chemoattraction are similar, changing by approximately 4% per second, as measured by L-serine addition and removal experiments.
results.evaluation: Claim C77 is supported by CIRA experiments with L-serine addition and removal (Figure 5F). This provides insight into the dynamics of chemotactic responses but is a relatively minor technical observation supporting the broader findings about serum taxis.

results.result: Enterobacteriaceae clinical isolates exhibit rapid chemotactic attraction toward femtoliter volumes of human serum in a novel microfluidics-based assay (CIRA). The bacterial population doubles near the serum source by 40 s, reaches maximal attraction by 90 s, and approaches equilibrium by 300 s. The CIRA system establishes steep microgradients where millimolar sources recede to nanomolar concentrations across hundreds of microns.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm these findings, stating 'the data are compelling' and describing the work as 'well executed' with 'novel chemotaxis assays [that] provide advantages in terms of temporal resolution and ability to detect responses from small concentrations.' One reviewer notes the authors 'present solid evidence that both lab and clinical Salmonella enterica serovars rapidly migrate towards human serum using an exciting approach.'

results.result: Chemotaxis mediates bacterial attraction to serum, with the chemoreceptor Tsr playing a significant but not exclusive role. The tsr mutant shows reduced but not absent attraction to serum, indicating multiple chemoreceptors and chemoattractants are involved. In competition experiments, wildtype outcompetes cheY mutants by 70-fold and tsr mutants by 3:1.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm that 'the behavior utilizes the bacterial chemotaxis system and the chemoreceptor Tsr.' One reviewer notes 'the authors do not adequately support their decision to focus exclusively on the Tsr receptor' and states 'Tsr is one of the chemoreceptors responsible for observed attraction to serum, but perhaps, not the receptor,' which aligns with the authors' own conclusion that multiple receptors are involved. The competitive advantage data is accepted without challenge.

results.result: L-serine is the primary chemoattractant in serum recognized by Tsr. Human serum contains ~241 µM L-serine, which is >200-fold greater than the minimal concentration (0.5-5 µM) required to elicit chemoattraction. The tsr mutant shows no attraction to L-serine but retains chemotaxis to L-aspartate. L-serine functions as a molecular cue directing bacteria toward serum, while other nutrients provide major growth advantages.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly state the work shows 'the chemoreceptor Tsr, which senses the amino acid L-serine' and describe this as providing 'a novel context for the role of serine as a bacterial chemoattractant.' One reviewer acknowledges 'it is perhaps not surprising these bacteria respond to serum as it is known to contain high levels of known chemoattractants, serine certainly,' which implicitly accepts the L-serine findings. The serine racemase experiment is noted as 'strong evidence that chemotaxis towards serine is responsible for the reduced attraction of the tsr mutant.'

results.result: Treatment of serum with serine racemase diminishes bacterial attraction, providing evidence that L-serine chemotaxis is responsible for Tsr-mediated serum attraction rather than pleiotropic effects.
results.evaluation: A reviewer explicitly notes this as a major strength: 'The authors show that the competitive advantage of WT cells relative to a tsr mutant is removed when serum is treated with serine-racemase and this provides strong evidence that chemotaxis towards serine is responsible for the reduced attraction of the tsr mutant (i.e. rather than any possible pleiotropic effects).'

results.result: S. Typhimurium shows no chemoattraction response to norepinephrine (NE) or DHMA, and these compounds show no binding to SeTsr LBD by ITC. NE and DHMA are thought to circulate at ~10 nM in serum.
results.evaluation: One reviewer raises significant concerns: 'Both norepinephrine (NE) and DHMA have been shown previously by other groups to be strong chemoattractants for E. coli (Ec), and that this behavior was mediated by Tsr... Given the 82% sequence identity between the Se and Ec Tsr, this finding is unexpected.' The reviewer requests testing E. coli in the assay and states 'currently the data is not strong enough to rule out Tsr as a receptor to these ligands in all cases.' Another reviewer notes the authors 'now include additional data to back up the intriguing lack of a movement response towards norepinephrine and DHMA,' suggesting the data has been strengthened but uncertainty remains.

results.result: The first crystal structures of S. Typhimurium Tsr LBD in complex with L-serine were solved at 2.2 Å and 2.5 Å resolution. The structure reveals the correct orientation of L-serine in the binding pocket, which differs from the previously published E. coli Tsr structure. L-serine binds with KD ~5 µM and forms specific hydrogen bonding interactions with conserved residues.
results.evaluation: One reviewer explicitly states they are 'not well placed to review the protein structural aspects of this work.' Another reviewer challenges the interpretation: 'I agree that the SeTsr ligand binding mode in the new structure is well-defined and unambiguous, but I think it is too strong to imply that the pose of the ligand in the previous structure is wrong. The two conformations are in fact quite similar to one another and the resolution of the older structure, is, in my view, insufficient to distinguish them.' The reviewer suggests alternative explanations including temperature effects and notes 'the current data is not convincing enough to say that a previous "misconception" is being corrected.'

results.result: A conserved amino acid recognition motif for L-serine is shared among Tsr orthologues. No experimentally determined structure for S. enterica Tsr had been published prior to this work.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these structural claims. The statement about no prior S. enterica Tsr structure is accepted as factual context, and the conservation analysis is not questioned.

results.result: Tsr is widely conserved among Enterobacteriaceae, Gammaproteobacteria, and numerous WHO priority pathogens associated with bloodstream infections, as determined by genomic database analysis.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm the generality findings, with one noting 'They illustrate the generality of their findings through phylogenetic analysis... Their interdisciplinary approach here greatly increases the scope of their findings.' The bioinformatics analysis identifying Tsr in WHO priority pathogens is accepted without challenge.

results.result: E. coli MG1655 and C. koseri BAA-895 exhibit attraction to human serum on timescales and magnitudes similar to Salmonella experiments.
results.evaluation: A reviewer explicitly notes as a strength: 'testing additional species within the Enterobacteriaceae family... Their interdisciplinary approach here greatly increases the scope of their findings.' The data showing other Enterobacteriaceae species respond to serum is accepted as supporting the generality of the phenomenon.

results.result: Horse and pig serum induce rapid attraction of S. Typhimurium similar to human serum, suggesting the phenomenon is relevant to diverse host-microbe systems. Swine share many aspects of human gastrointestinal physiology.
results.evaluation: A reviewer explicitly identifies this as a major strength: 'New experimental data showing Salmonella enterica is also attracted to swine and equine serum (including an ex vivo swine model) is a useful addition that hints at the potential generality of the response reported here.' The cross-species serum attraction data is accepted as supporting broader relevance.

results.result: Enterobacteriaceae use human serum as a source of nutrients for growth. Serum addition enhances growth of all Salmonella strains surveyed, with 2.5% v/v serum providing 1.5-2.5-fold growth increase.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge the growth data. One reviewer notes 'it is perhaps not surprising these bacteria respond to serum as it is known to contain high levels of known chemoattractants,' which implicitly accepts that serum provides nutritional benefits. The growth enhancement data is presented without reviewer objection.

results.result: Chemotaxis and Tsr provide a competitive advantage for migration into enterohemorrhagic lesions in an ex vivo swine colonic model. Wildtype outcompetes cheY mutants ~10:1 and tsr mutants ~2:1, with bacteria penetrating >200 µm into wounded vasculature.
results.evaluation: A reviewer identifies a significant weakness: 'The addition of an ex vivo swine model is an exciting new inclusion in the updated manuscript. However, information regarding biological and technical replication here is currently unclear or missing.' While the ex vivo data is described as 'exciting,' the lack of clear replication information creates uncertainty about the robustness of the competitive advantage findings. Another reviewer questions whether 'the work does not establish the physiological relevance of the behavior or associate it with any type of disease progression.'

results.result: The authors define 'bacterial vampirism' as bacterial taxis toward serum, colonization of hemorrhagic lesions, and consumption of serum nutrients, proposing this may relate to the proclivity of Enterobacteriaceae for bloodstream infections. They suggest this aligns with emerging understanding of how chemotaxis drives tropism for damaged tissue.
results.evaluation: One reviewer explicitly states 'the work does not establish the physiological relevance of the behavior or associate it with any type of disease progression' and notes 'the impact of this finding on the chemotaxis or medical fields is uncertain.' Another reviewer describes the work as having 'clinical implications for bacterial bloodstream invasion during episodes of gastrointestinal bleeding,' suggesting some acceptance of the broader relevance. However, the speculative nature of connecting the ex vivo findings to in vivo disease progression remains a point of uncertainty.

results.result: Background claims about Enterobacteriaceae association with GI bleeding, bacteremia, and sepsis in IBD patients; epidemiology of GI bleeding; and prior findings about L-serine in colitis models and Tsr-mediated invasion of Peyer's patches.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these background claims, which are supported by citations to established literature. One reviewer notes the work 'could have clinical implications for bacterial bloodstream invasion during episodes of gastrointestinal bleeding,' implicitly accepting the clinical context. Another describes the work as 'documenting what is likely to be a key step in bloodstream entry for some of the main sepsis-associated pathogens during gastrointestinal bleeding.'

comparisons.comparison: Both strongly support claims about Enterobacteriaceae attraction to serum using CIRA methodology (C3-C4, C20-C26, C78-C81). Peer reviewers explicitly describe the data as 'compelling' and 'well executed,' fully aligning with OpenEval's assessment of robust evidence with appropriate controls.

Both support chemotaxis mechanism claims (C5, C27-C29, C74-C76, C92). OpenEval and peer reviewers agree that cheY mutant data definitively establishes chemotaxis as the mechanism. Peer review notes some uncertainty about exclusive focus on Tsr, which aligns with both evaluations acknowledging multiple receptors are involved.

Both support L-serine as the key chemoattractant (C6-C7, C34-C38, C43, C73). Peer reviewers describe this as 'novel context' and explicitly praise the serine racemase experiment as 'strong evidence,' matching OpenEval's assessment of converging evidence lines including mass spectrometry, dose-response, and genetic specificity.

Both address serine racemase experiment (C30). Peer reviewer R4 explicitly highlights this as major strength providing 'strong evidence that chemotaxis towards serine is responsible for the reduced attraction of the tsr mutant,' fully aligning with OpenEval R3's assessment of this experiment as part of converging evidence for L-serine specificity.

Significant disagreement on NE/DHMA negative results (C50-C51). OpenEval finds the negative data convincing given thoroughness of testing. Peer reviewers express uncertainty, noting the findings are 'unexpected' given prior E. coli literature and stating 'currently the data is not strong enough to rule out Tsr as a receptor to these ligands in all cases.'

Overlap on serine quantification claims (C32-C33). OpenEval R3 supports these as part of converging L-serine evidence. Peer R5 groups these with NE/DHMA negative results and expresses uncertainty about the overall conclusion, though the mass spec data itself is not directly challenged.

Disagreement on structural claims (C8, C46-C49, C82-C87, C89). OpenEval finds crystallographic data supports the structure and correction of prior work. Peer reviewers express uncertainty: one states they are 'not well placed to review' structural aspects, another challenges that 'it is too strong to imply that the pose of the ligand in the previous structure is wrong,' suggesting the two conformations are 'quite similar.'

Both address detailed structural characterization (C63-C68). OpenEval strongly supports the electron density analysis and paired refinement validation. Peer reviewers express uncertainty about whether this truly corrects a 'misconception,' with one noting the resolution of the older structure may be 'insufficient to distinguish' the conformations and suggesting alternative explanations.

Both support phylogenetic and conservation analysis claims (C10-C11, C52-C53). OpenEval finds the genomic database analysis comprehensive. Peer reviewers affirm the generality findings, with one noting the 'interdisciplinary approach here greatly increases the scope of their findings.' Full alignment on these bioinformatics claims.

Both support structural novelty claim (C9). OpenEval notes this as factual context for the study. Peer reviewers accept this without challenge as background information. Minor overlap with full agreement.

Both support testing of additional Enterobacteriaceae species (C54-C55). OpenEval includes this in overall assessment of robust attraction evidence. Peer reviewers explicitly praise 'testing additional species' as a strength that 'greatly increases the scope of their findings.'

Both support cross-species serum attraction (C56-C57). OpenEval includes swine and equine serum data in overall evidence for serum attraction. Peer reviewers identify this as 'major strength' and 'useful addition that hints at the potential generality of the response.'

Both support growth data claims (C12, C39-C40). OpenEval finds growth curve experiments support the inference that L-serine functions primarily as chemotactic cue. Peer reviewers do not challenge the growth data, with one implicitly accepting nutritional benefits by noting serum contains 'high levels of known chemoattractants.'

Both address ex vivo competitive advantage (C13, C58-C60), but with different levels of confidence. OpenEval supports the data but notes limited replicates and cautions about extrapolation to in vivo infection. Peer reviewers describe the ex vivo model as 'exciting' but express uncertainty due to 'unclear or missing' information on biological and technical replication.

Both express uncertainty about physiological relevance and disease progression claims (C14-C15, C61, C95-C96, C99-C100). OpenEval notes these represent 'conceptual synthesis and speculation' with insufficient evidence for causality in disease. Peer reviewers similarly state 'the work does not establish the physiological relevance of the behavior or associate it with any type of disease progression,' though some accept potential clinical implications.

Both support background/contextual claims from literature (C1-C2, C17-C19, C70). OpenEval notes these represent established medical knowledge with appropriate citations. Peer reviewers do not challenge these claims, implicitly accepting the clinical context for the study.

Both support literature-based contextual claims (C16, C42, C62, C69, C72, C91, C93-C94, C97-C98). OpenEval finds these provide appropriate context and rationale. Peer reviewers accept these background claims without challenge, with some describing potential 'clinical implications for bacterial bloodstream invasion.'

Minor overlap on L-serine dynamics (C77). OpenEval R13 notes this as supporting technical observation about chemotactic response dynamics. Peer R3 includes this among L-serine evidence without specific comment. Both implicitly support this minor claim.

Partial overlap on L-serine functional role (C41, C44). OpenEval R7 addresses L-serine as chemotactic cue vs. growth substrate. Peer R3 focuses on L-serine as chemoattractant without specifically addressing the growth substrate distinction, though both support L-serine's chemotactic function.

Minor overlap on cross-species relevance (C90). OpenEval R9 includes this in speculative claims about broader pathogenesis. Peer R10 addresses cross-species serum data as supporting generality. Both touch on broader applicability but in different contexts.
Minor overlap on literature context (C91). OpenEval R12 includes this as background citation. Peer R10 addresses cross-species experimental data. Minimal substantive overlap beyond claim ID.

Minor overlap on literature context (C72). OpenEval R12 includes this as background citation about chemotaxis. Peer R5 focuses on NE/DHMA negative results with uncertainty. Minimal substantive connection.
Minor overlap on literature context (C42). OpenEval R12 includes this as background citation. Peer R3 addresses L-serine experimental evidence. Minimal substantive overlap.
